Bootstrap sampling

Source: R/design-bootstrap.R
design_bootstrap.Rd

Generates bootstrap replicates. "simple" resamples rows independently. "block" is the moving-block bootstrap (Künsch 1989), which keeps the serial dependence in ordered data by concatenating ceiling(n / block_length) runs of block_length consecutive rows per replicate, each starting at a row chosen at random. A run must fit inside the frame, so fewer runs cover the first and last block_length - 1 rows, and the first row and the last turn up only 1 / block_length as often as a row in the middle. "circular" (Politis and Romano 1992) joins the last row to the first, so a run can wrap around the end and every row turns up equally often on average.

Usage

design_bootstrap(
  n_replicates = 1000L,
  n = NULL,
  method = c("simple", "block", "circular"),
  block_length = NULL,
  output = c("rows", "indices", "weights")
)

Arguments

n_replicates

Number of replicates to generate.

n

Rows per replicate. NULL uses nrow(data), the standard nonparametric bootstrap. n = 0 gives replicates with no rows. The frame then has no rows but keeps its .replicate column, so split() returns no replicates at all, while split(out, factor(out$.replicate, seq_len(n_replicates))) returns n_replicates empty ones. A plan from plan_size() gives its n.

method

"simple", "block" or "circular".

block_length

Run length for method = "block" and "circular", and an error for method = "simple", where it would have no effect. NULL uses floor(nrow(data)^(1/3)), a common rule of thumb.

output

What draw() returns.

  • "rows", the default, returns the resampled rows of every replicate in one data frame, with a leading .replicate column.

  • "indices" returns an integer matrix with n rows and a column per replicate, holding the rows of data that each replicate drew, in order. Row i of replicate r is data[out[i, r], ].

  • "weights" returns an integer matrix with a row for each row of data and a column per replicate, holding the number of times each replicate drew that row. With the default n, these are replicate weights for survey::svrepdesign(type = "bootstrap", combined.weights = TRUE).

For one seed, all three hold the same replicates.

Value

A design object, for use with draw().

Details

By default draw() returns all replicates in one data frame with a leading .replicate column. Split them with split(out, out$.replicate). That frame holds n_replicates * n rows, a copy of the data for each replicate, and draw() warns, with class drawn_bootstrap_size, when it would exceed 10 million rows. output = "indices" and output = "weights" return the same replicates as a matrix instead.

Not a survey design

The bootstrap resamples the data you already have to approximate the sampling distribution of a statistic (Efron 1979). It is not a probability sample of a finite population, so it has no inclusion probabilities and cannot be passed to ht_total(). For the design-based variance of a total or mean, use the estimators there.

Resampling rows treats them as independent draws from one distribution. For such data and a statistic those estimators do not cover, such as a median, the bootstrap is the standard tool. A sample drawn with strata or clusters is not such data, and resampling its rows one by one ignores the strata and treats the rows of a cluster as independent. Resample the clusters within strata instead, for example with survey::as.svrepdesign(as_svydesign(s), type = "subbootstrap"). Runs of rows keep short-range dependence in ordered data (Künsch 1989).

References

Efron, B. (1979). Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife. Annals of Statistics, 7, 1–26. doi:10.1214/aos/1176344552

Künsch, H. R. (1989). The jackknife and the bootstrap for general stationary observations. Annals of Statistics, 17, 1217–1241. doi:10.1214/aos/1176347265

Politis, D. N. and Romano, J. P. (1992). A circular block-resampling procedure for stationary data. In R. LePage and L. Billard (eds.), Exploring the Limits of Bootstrap, 263–270. Wiley.

See also

draw()

Other designs: design_certainty(), design_cluster(), design_multistage(), design_reservoir(), design_simple(), design_spatial(), design_spread(), design_stratified(), design_systematic(), design_temporal(), design_weighted()

Examples

df <- data.frame(id = 1:100, value = (1:100) / 10)

reps <- draw(df, design_bootstrap(n_replicates = 5, n = 20), seed = 1)
table(reps$.replicate)
#> 
#>  1  2  3  4  5 
#> 20 20 20 20 20 

# A statistic per replicate
vapply(split(reps, reps$.replicate), function(r) mean(r$value), numeric(1))
#>     1     2     3     4     5 
#> 5.450 5.285 4.395 4.735 5.570 

# The same replicates as row numbers, without copying the data
idx <- draw(df, design_bootstrap(n_replicates = 5, n = 20,
                                 output = "indices"), seed = 1)
apply(idx, 2, function(i) mean(df$value[i]))
#> [1] 5.450 5.285 4.395 4.735 5.570

# Runs of 10 rows that may wrap from the last row to the first
circ <- draw(df, design_bootstrap(n_replicates = 200, method = "circular",
                                  block_length = 10, output = "weights"),
             seed = 1)
range(rowMeans(circ))
#> [1] 0.910 1.185
